content:
We have carbon NMR data: list of chemical shifts. Need number of methyl (CH3) groups. Methyl carbons typically appear around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but also 20-30. In data we have peaks: 168.30 (likely carbonyl), 130.70,130.27,128.35,126.66,124.85,123.57 (aromatic), 58.70 (maybe O-CH3 or CH2 attached to hetero), 36.40 (twice), 26.40.

Methyl groups: aliphatic CH3 appear ~10-30 ppm. Here we have 26.40 likely a methyl. 36.40 could be CH2 or CH3 attached to something like carbonyl? 36 ppm is typical for CH2 next to carbonyl or CH3 attached to aromatic? But methyl attached to aromatic (toluene) appears ~20 ppm. 36 is more like CH2. 58.70 is likely O-CH3 (methoxy) which is a methyl attached to O, appears ~55 ppm. So that's also a methyl (OCH3). So we have at least two methyl groups: one at 26.4 (alkyl) and one at 58.7 (methoxy). The 36.40 peaks could be CH2 (two of them). So total methyl groups = 2.

But need to be sure: Could 36.40 be methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl) ~30 ppm. But 36 is a bit high. However we have two identical peaks at 36.40, could be two equivalent methyls? If they are equivalent, they'd be same shift. Could be two methyl groups attached to same environment (e.g., two acetyl groups). But we also have 26.40 distinct. So maybe there are three methyls total: 58.7 (OCH3), 36.4 (two equivalent methyls), 26.4 (another methyl). However 36 ppm for methyl attached to aromatic (para-methyl) is ~21 ppm, not 36. For methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl) ~30 ppm. 36 could be a CH2. The fact there are two identical peaks suggests two carbons in same environment, could be two CH2 groups (e.g., ethylene glycol). But CH2 typically ~30-40 ppm. So likely CH2.

Thus methyl count = 2.

We could also get proton NMR to confirm number of methyl protons. Let's get proton NMR.
